Lisbon in October (Portugal in the Fall)

Antonina Pattiz | September 1, 2026 | Leave a Comment

Listen to audio version of this article
Sponsored by
0:00 / 14:32
Instaread

Lisbon has my heart, and October is when I stop pretending otherwise. My husband and I have been back to this city more times than I can count, in nearly every month it offers, and the trips I replay most are always the October ones. The light goes soft and gold. The August crush of visitors thins out. And the whole place seems to exhale, like a host who has finally gotten the party under control and can pour themselves a glass.

  • Yes, You Can Still Swim (Sort Of)

Here is the short version. October in Lisbon runs to daytime highs around 73 degrees Fahrenheit, the Atlantic is still warm enough for a quick, bracing swim if you are brave, the wine harvest has just wrapped and the tastings are pouring, and you can walk the seven hills without soaking your shirt. Portugal spends July and August sweating through its shirt. In October, it dries off and shows off.

The Weather Is the Whole Reason

Let me be specific, because vague promises of “nice weather” are worthless when you are booking flights. October in Lisbon averages a daytime high of about 73 degrees Fahrenheit and dips to around 59 at night. You will want a light jacket after sunset. During the day, in the sun, on a south-facing miradouro, it can feel warmer than that, and I have peeled down to a t-shirt in late October more than once.

The catch, and there is always a catch, is rain. October is when the autumn rains start to return after the bone-dry summer. Expect somewhere around a dozen rainy days across the month and roughly three inches of rain total. That sounds worse than it plays. Most of it comes in short, dramatic bursts rather than gray all-day drizzle, and I have had entire October weeks in Lisbon without opening my umbrella once. Early October is the safer bet if rain would ruin your trip. Pack a compact umbrella and stop worrying about it.

Daylight is generous too. You get around eleven hours of it and about seven hours of sunshine on an average day. That is enough to fit in a morning at a palace, an afternoon at the beach, and a long dinner without ever feeling rushed by the dark. If you want the full breakdown of how the seasons stack up, I wrote an honest month-by-month guide to the best time to visit Lisbon that spells out exactly which weeks I would book and which I would skip.

Yes, You Can Still Swim (Sort Of)

Here is where I have to be honest with you, because the internet loves to oversell the “swimmable Atlantic in October” line. The sea temperature off Lisbon in October hovers around 67 to 68 degrees Fahrenheit. That is not warm. That is the kind of water that makes you gasp on entry and then, three minutes later, feels absolutely glorious.

Portuguese locals swim in this without blinking. My husband and I have run into the water at Carcavelos in early October, shrieked like children, and come out grinning. If you grew up on the bathtub-warm Mediterranean or a Florida beach, it will feel cold to you. If you are an Oregonian like me, used to a coastline that never really warms up, it feels downright generous. Manage your expectations, and it is a genuine treat. The upside of the cooler water is that the beaches are gorgeous and half-empty. In August the sand at Carcavelos disappears under towels. In October you can spread out.

The train from Cais do Sodre station runs straight along the coast to Carcavelos, Estoril, and Cascais, and October is when that ride is at its most beautiful. Fewer crowds, calmer light, dramatic skies rolling in off the ocean. Which brings me to the town at the end of the line.

Cascais and the Coast Are at Their Best

Cascais is a former fishing village turned genteel seaside resort about 40 minutes west of Lisbon by train, and it is my favorite easy escape from the city. In summer it is packed to the gills. In October it goes back to feeling like the relaxed coastal town it actually is. You can walk the promenade, poke around the old center, sit at a cafe over a plate of grilled fish, and watch the Atlantic do its thing without fighting a crowd for a table.

The cliffs at Boca do Inferno are a short walk from town, and the whole coastline gets more dramatic in autumn as the swells pick up. If you want a proper day of it, I put together a full guide to the best things to do in Cascais with the spots we return to every time. Bring a jacket for the sea breeze, which has real teeth by late afternoon.

This Is Harvest Season, and the Wine Is Everywhere

If you care even a little about wine, October is the month to come. The Portuguese grape harvest, the vindima, runs from late August through October depending on the region, which means that when you arrive the cellars are full and everyone is in a celebratory mood. The wine region right around Lisbon, plus the Setubal Peninsula just across the river, runs tastings and cellar tours all through the harvest window.

You do not even have to leave the city to drink well. Lisbon is stacked with tiny wine bars where a knowledgeable pour costs a few euros, and in October the by-the-glass lists lean into the fresh, young, still-fizzing new wines. Order a vinho verde, which is meant to be drunk young and slightly sparkling, and you are tasting the season in a glass. My husband and I have a standing habit of finding a hole-in-the-wall wine bar in Alfama, ordering whatever the owner recommends, and letting the evening go where it wants.

There is usually a proper wine event in the mix too. In recent years the big Lisbon wine fair Vinhos and Sabores has landed in mid-to-late October at the international fairgrounds, pouring hundreds of Portuguese labels under one roof. Dates shift year to year, so check the current calendar before you count on it, but the point stands. October is when Portuguese wine takes a bow.

The Crowds Thin and the City Comes Back to Itself

This is the part I love most, and it is hard to put a number on. October is shoulder season, which means the enormous summer wave has receded but the city has not gone quiet. Restaurants are still lively. Trams still run. But you can get a table at the places that were impossible in July, and you can climb into a miradouro without elbowing for railing space.

The famous Tram 28 is a good barometer. In peak summer the line to board it stretches around the block and you spend the ride wedged against strangers. In October you can actually get a seat, look out the window, and enjoy the rattling climb through Alfama and Graca the way it is meant to be enjoyed. Same with the viewpoints. The miradouros are where Lisbon shows off, and I have a whole rundown of the best viewpoints in Lisbon if you want to plan a sunset crawl across the hills. In October the golden hour is early enough that you can catch it and still make dinner.

Fair warning though. October is only shoulder season for beach tourism. It is still very much high season for one thing, and that thing is Sintra.

Sintra in October (The One Thing to Book Ahead)

Sintra, the fairy-tale hill town of palaces and gardens about 40 minutes from Lisbon, is genuinely better in autumn. The forested hills are lush, the light through the trees is gorgeous, and the cooler air makes the endless walking up and down between sites far more pleasant than it is in the summer heat. Pena Palace, the candy-colored royal palace on the peak, looks incredible against a moody October sky.

But here is the honest downside, and it is a real one. Sintra stays busy in October, especially on weekends. This is not a place where the crowds evaporate the way they do at the beach. Book your Pena Palace timed-entry ticket online in advance, go early in the day, and go on a weekday if you possibly can. We learned that one the hard way, showing up on a Saturday morning without tickets and spending our first hour in a line instead of a garden. Foolish. Do not repeat our mistake.

If you have the time, give Sintra a full day rather than cramming it into an afternoon. I mapped out exactly how I would spend it in my one day in Sintra itinerary, built around beating the crowds and seeing the two or three sites that actually earn the hype rather than trying to do all of them.

What to Actually Do in the City

October weather is perfect for the thing Lisbon does best, which is reward you for wandering. This is a city built for walking, if your knees can handle the hills, and the mild autumn air is exactly right for it. One of my favorite spots in any season is the Carmo Convent, the roofless Gothic church left open to the sky after the great 1755 earthquake. Its bare stone arches frame the blue like a cathedral for the clouds, and in October the light pours straight down into the nave. It is one of the most quietly moving places in the city, and it is right in the middle of Chiado.

Beyond that, the usual greats hold up beautifully in the shoulder-season quiet. The Jeronimos Monastery and the Belem Tower out in Belem, the maze of Alfama, a pastel de nata eaten warm and dusted with cinnamon while it is still too hot to hold comfortably. If you want a tight, opinionated plan, I laid out a full list of things to do in Lisbon that separates the genuinely worth-it from the tourist-trap filler. And if you are only in town for two or three days, my perfect weekend in Lisbon guide sequences it all so you are not backtracking across the hills.

Chestnuts, Cinnamon, and the Smell of Autumn

By the back end of October, the roasted chestnut carts start appearing on the streets. This is a real Lisbon autumn ritual, tied to the feast of Sao Martinho in early November, and once it starts the whole downtown begins to smell faintly of smoke and sweetness. Vendors roast castanhas over charcoal in little metal drums near Rossio square and along Avenida da Liberdade, and a paper cone of hot chestnuts on a cool evening is one of those small perfect things. If you come in late October you will catch the very start of it. Come the first week of November and you will be in the thick of it.

The food in general leans autumnal and hearty this time of year. Rich seafood stews, grilled fish, caldo verde soup, and the wine to match all of it. After a summer of light salads and cold drinks, Lisbon’s cooler-weather cooking is a genuine pleasure.

The Honest Downsides

I would be doing you a disservice if I only sold you the golden light. So here is the plain truth about the trade-offs.

The rain is real. If you have your heart set on beach days, October is a gamble, and a rained-out afternoon is more likely here than in July. Build in flexibility and have a museum or two in your back pocket for the wet days. The sea is cold, as I said, so if “swimmable Atlantic” was your only reason to come, adjust your expectations to “a quick invigorating dip” rather than lazy hours floating in warm water. And Sintra stays crowded, so it demands planning that the rest of your trip does not.

None of that would keep me away. If anything, the mix of warm-enough days, thinning crowds, harvest wine, and that particular slant of autumn light makes October the version of Lisbon I would send a first-timer to, no hesitation. It is the city with its guard down and its best foot forward at the same time.

Frequently Asked Questions

Is October a good time to visit Lisbon?
October is one of the best times to visit Lisbon. Daytime highs sit around 73 degrees Fahrenheit, the summer crowds have thinned, prices ease off their peak, and the grape harvest means the wine bars are pouring their best. The main trade-off is a higher chance of rain than in summer.

Can you swim in Lisbon in October?
You can, though the Atlantic runs around 67 to 68 degrees Fahrenheit, which is bracing rather than balmy. Locals swim happily, and the beaches at Carcavelos, Estoril, and Cascais are far less crowded than in summer. Expect a quick, invigorating dip rather than warm-water lounging.

What is the weather like in Lisbon in October?
Mild and mostly sunny, with average highs near 73 degrees Fahrenheit and lows around 59. You get roughly seven hours of sunshine a day and about eleven hours of daylight. Rain returns after the dry summer, so expect around a dozen rainy days across the month, usually in short bursts.

What should I pack for Lisbon in October?
Layers. Comfortable walking shoes for the hills, a light jacket for cooler evenings and the coastal breeze, a compact umbrella for the odd rainy day, and a swimsuit if you plan to brave the ocean. Sunglasses too, because the midday sun is still strong.

October is Lisbon at its most generous, and I will happily keep coming back to prove it. If you go, find yourself a little wine bar at dusk, order whatever the owner points at, and watch the light do its thing over the rooftops. You will understand why this city has my heart.

Cheers!
Antonina
